title: Asymptotic Analysis of Empirical Risk Minimization on Entry-wise i.i.d. Heavy-Tailed Data
authors: Kaito Takanami, Takashi Takahashi, Yoshiyuki Kabashima
abstract: Many real-world datasets exhibit unusually large values far more frequently than predicted by Gaussian models. Heavy-tailed distributions capture this behavior, yet evaluating learning performance under them remains challenging because rare, large feature entries retain non-vanishing effects even in high dimensions. Even in the canonical setting of empirical risk minimization for linear regression with entry-wise i.i.d. symmetric $α$-stable data, a precise asymptotic characterization of prediction has been lacking. In this work, we introduce a functional order parameter that describes the random effective problem associated with each coefficient. Using the replica method, we fully characterize the generalization error in the proportional high-dimensional limit where the sample size and feature dimension diverge at a fixed ratio. Additionally, this analysis establishes a heavy-tail universality law, scaling laws relating typical errors to prediction reliability, and the Bayes-optimal prediction error. In addition to characterizing the effects of extreme entries on the learning process, our method applies broadly to other systems with persistent local heterogeneity.
summary: This work provides a rigorous asymptotic analysis of machine learning performance when data features follow heavy-tailed $\alpha$-stable distributions. By employing the replica method, the authors characterize the generalization error, establishing a universal scaling law dependent only on the tail index $\alpha$. This is crucial for understanding reliable inference in real-world datasets with extreme outliers.
main_problem: The paper characterizes the asymptotic generalization error of Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) when the input data features are heavy-tailed, specifically $\alpha$-stable.
main_result: It establishes a heavy-tail universality law, showing that the generalization error scales differently than in the Gaussian case, and provides scaling laws for typical prediction errors.
method: The analysis heavily employs the replica method from statistical physics to reduce the complex high-dimensional optimization problem to an effective one-dimensional problem characterized by a functional order parameter.
model_or_system: The model is high-dimensional linear regression where the training inputs are assumed to be entry-wise i.i.d. $\alpha$-stable distributed, contrasting with standard Gaussian assumptions.
key_observables: Generalization error $E^{(\alpha)}_{N,D}$, test prediction error $\Delta^{(\alpha)}_{N,D}$, and the functional order parameter $\hat{P}$.
important_parameters: The tail index $\alpha$ ($0 < \alpha < 2$), the sample-to-dimension ratio $\kappa = N/D$, and the functional order parameter $\hat{P}$.
main_assumptions: The loss function $\ell$ must be convex, and the analysis relies on the proportional high-dimensional limit ($N/D 	o \kappa$).
figures_summary: Figures validate the theoretical predictions for the limiting coefficient error $q_{\alpha}$ across various ratios $\kappa$ and tail indices $\alpha$, comparing theoretical lines to numerical results.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first defining the ERM problem for heavy-tailed data, introducing the functional order parameter, and then using the replica method to derive asymptotic results, culminating in establishing universality laws and comparing entry-wise vs. elliptical models.
why_interesting: While the core is statistical learning theory, the use of the replica method and the analysis of high-dimensional random matrices/optimization problems share deep mathematical techniques with disordered systems and spin glass models.
